name: Gossip & reputation spreading
human_example:
In tight-knit communities, word spreads fast about who isn't pulling their weight. A 2012 study found gossip about free-riders travels faster than direct observation — and deters cheating effectively.

Feinberg, M. et al. (2012) 'Gossip and ostracism promote cooperation in groups.' Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612443403
key_references: Feinberg et al. (2012) Psychological Science; Nowak & Sigmund (2005) Nature (indirect reciprocity / image scoring)
llm_evidence: Implicit in GovSim & SanctSim (agents see others' history); gossip not isolated as mechanism.

name: Reputation score / credit system
human_example:
Your Uber driver rating, eBay seller feedback, or social credit score — a running number that unlocks or restricts access based on track record. Drop below a threshold and you lose privileges automatically.

Dellarocas, C. (2003) 'The digitization of word of mouth.' Management Science. https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.49.10.1407.17308
key_references: Dellarocas (2003) Management Science; Uber/eBay ratings; China social credit
llm_evidence: SanctSim provides running contribution records visible to all group members.

name: Cryptographic audit log / immutable transparency
human_example:
A permanent, tamper-proof record — every action logged and attributable forever. Not a punishment itself, but makes punishment possible by guaranteeing detection. Sanction-enabler: you can't enforce norms you can't see.

Nakamoto, S. (2008) Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System. https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf Also Pierucci, F. et al. (2026) governance graph paper (preprint). | Every government spending decision published in an open ledger anyone can check. Blockchain-based municipal transparency projects use this. Makes defection costly through permanent visibility — 'sunlight as disinfectant'.

Kolt, N. (2024) 'Governing AI Agents.' Arizona Law Review. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4772652 Also Ostrom's P4 (monitoring must be present for sanctions to work).
key_references: Nakamoto (2008) Bitcoin whitepaper; Kolt (2024) Governing AI Agents; Pierucci et al. (2026) governance graphs
llm_evidence: GovSim provides full extraction histories. Kolt (2024) formalises as 'visibility principle'.

name: Ostracism, exile & social shunning
human_example:
Temporary or permanent exclusion — from a village, a platform, or a trade network. Lab experiments show even the threat of expulsion nearly doubles cooperation in public goods games.

Cinyabuguma, M. et al. (2005) 'Cooperation under the threat of expulsion in a public goods experiment.' J. of Economic Behavior & Org. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2005.02.010
key_references: Cinyabuguma et al. (2005) JEBO; Gürerk et al. (2006) Science
llm_evidence: SanctSim implements exclusion from sanctioning institution for poor contributors.

name: Suspension of access / licence revocation
human_example:
Temporarily losing access to the shared resource — your fishing licence suspended for a season, or locked out of an irrigation channel. Time-limited exclusion that signals seriousness without being permanent.

Baland, J.M. & Platteau, J.P. (1996) Halting Degradation of Natural Resources. FAO/Clarendon Press.
key_references: Baland & Platteau (1996) Halting Degradation; Ostrom (1990) graduated sanctions
llm_evidence: GovSim: resource depletion ends agent's access. Explicit time-limited exclusion not implemented.

name: Allowlist / denylist
human_example:
Email spam filters (Spamhaus blocklist) — once flagged, no one receives your messages. Binary, automatic exclusion with no gradation. Fast and scalable but can catch legitimate senders in friendly fire.

Ramachandran, A. & Feamster, N. (2006) 'Understanding the network-level behavior of spammers.' ACM SIGCOMM. https://doi.org/10.1145/1151659.1159939
key_references: Ramachandran & Feamster (2006) SIGCOMM; email spam filters (Spamhaus)
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM systems.

name: Ridicule, shaming & social disapproval
human_example:
The low-level embarrassment of showing up empty-handed to a potluck, or being the only one not contributing to a group gift. Subtle but powerful in close-knit groups — stigma is a cost even without formal rules.

Masclet, D. et al. (2003) 'Monetary and nonmonetary punishment in the voluntary contributions mechanism.' American Economic Review. https://doi.org/10.1257/000282803321455395
key_references: Masclet et al. (2003) AER (non-monetary punishment); Feinberg et al. (2012)
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. Informal disapproval not implemented as discrete mechanism.

name: Altruistic punishment (Fehr-Gächter)
human_example:
Humans will spend their own money to punish a stranger who cheated — even in a one-shot game where they'll never meet again. Fehr & Gächter proved this experimentally. Anger at unfairness, not self-interest, drives it.

Fehr, E. & Gächter, S. (2002) 'Altruistic punishment in humans.' Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/415137a
key_references: Fehr & Gächter (2002) Nature; Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim
llm_evidence: ✓ Directly tested (SanctSim). LLMs can pay 1 to impose −3. LLMs strongly avoid it vs. humans.

name: Fixed fine / traffic fine / auto-penalty
human_example:
A speed camera issues a fine automatically the moment you exceed the limit. No discretion, no negotiation — fast and cheap to administer. Automatic triggering means no cost of detection beyond the technology.

Mookherjee, D. & Png, I. (1994) 'Marginal deterrence in enforcement of law.' J. of Political Economy. https://doi.org/10.1086/261938
key_references: Mookherjee & Png (1994) JPE; Ostrom (1990)
llm_evidence: GovSim auto-deducts from over-extractors — functionally equivalent.

name: Pre-agreed contractual penalty (liquidated damages, penalty clause)
human_example:
A pre-agreed penalty for breach — like a builder who owes £500/day for every late day, agreed before work starts. Avoids court arguments about 'what harm did this actually cause?' by fixing the cost upfront.

Cavendish Square Holding BV v. Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67. https://www.supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2013-0280.html | A contract clause specifying a penalty for breach — enforceable in France or Germany even if the other party can't prove actual loss. Courts can reduce it if the amount seems grossly disproportionate.

Beale, H. et al. (2019) Ius Commune Casebooks on Contract Law. Hart Publishing. Also Council of Europe Resolution (71) 28. | In English and US law, a 'penalty' clause is void — but a 'liquidated damages' clause (a genuine pre-estimate of loss) is enforceable. Courts ask: was this a reasonable guess at likely harm, not a punishment?

Cavendish Square v. Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67. https://www.supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2013-0280.html
key_references: Cavendish Square v. Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67; Beale et al. (2019) Ius Commune
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM systems.
notes: merged Overview "Civil law penalty clause"; merged Overview "LD enforceable, penalty void"

name: Proof-of-stake slashing
human_example:
Ethereum validators lock up their own money ('stake') before they can participate. If they cheat — e.g. signing two conflicting blocks — the protocol automatically destroys part of that stake. Real skin in the game.

Buterin, V. et al. Ethereum Proof-of-Stake spec. https://ethereum.github.io/consensus-specs/ Also Saleh, F. (2021) 'Blockchain without waste.' Review of Financial Studies. https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhaa075
key_references: Ethereum PoS spec; Saleh (2021) RFS; EigenLayer restaking (correlated slash)
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM social dilemma context.

name: Sentencing guidelines (standardised formula)
human_example:
Standardised formula for deciding punishments — like US Federal Sentencing Guidelines — so similar crimes get similar sentences regardless of the judge. Reduces arbitrariness and improves perceived fairness.

US Sentencing Commission (2023) Guidelines Manual. https://www.ussc.gov/guidelines/2023-guidelines-manual
key_references: US Sentencing Commission (2023) Guidelines Manual
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Token toxicity (self-defeating attack cost)
human_example:
To attack the Ethereum network you'd need to buy 51% of all staked ETH — but buying that much drives up the price, and attacking the network destroys its value. The attacker defeats themselves. Self-defeating defection.

Buterin, V. (2014) Ethereum Whitepaper. https://ethereum.org/en/whitepaper/
key_references: Buterin (2014) Ethereum Whitepaper
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Restaking & correlated slash
human_example:
EigenLayer lets the same Ethereum stake secure multiple systems at once. If any of those systems detects misbehaviour, all stakes across all systems can be cut simultaneously — amplifying punishment for coordinated attacks.

EigenLayer (2023) Whitepaper: EigenLayer: The Restaking Collective. https://docs.eigenlayer.xyz/eigenlayer/overview/whitepaper
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM multi-agent social dilemma context.

name: Praise, status elevation & prestige
human_example:
Generous people get celebrated — hunters who share meat gain status; potlatch hosts earn community prestige. Henrich & Gil-White show prestige is a distinct human status mechanism that rewards contribution.

Henrich, J. & Gil-White, F. (2001) 'The evolution of prestige.' Evolution & Human Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1090-5138(00)00071-4
key_references: Henrich & Gil-White (2001) Evolution & Human Behavior; Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim
llm_evidence: Partially tested via SanctSim reward mechanism. LLMs strongly prefer rewards over punishment.

name: Pigouvian subsidy / grant for public good
human_example:
Government grants for solar panels pay you to do something socially good. Lab research found subsidies can be more efficient than fines in public goods contexts — especially when cooperation is already widespread.

Andreoni, J. et al. (2003) 'Carrot or stick: Rewards, punishments, and cooperation.' American Economic Review. https://doi.org/10.1257/000282803321455278
key_references: Andreoni et al. (2003) AER (carrot or stick); Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim
llm_evidence: ✓ Directly tested (SanctSim). LLMs use subsidies as primary enforcement tool.

name: Staking reward / validator yield
human_example:
Honest Ethereum validators earn around 3–5% annual yield on their staked ETH — paid automatically for doing their job correctly. The reward makes the threat of slashing credible: you have something real to lose.

Saleh, F. (2021) 'Blockchain without waste.' Review of Financial Studies. https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhaa075 Also Roughgarden, T. (2021) 'Transaction fee mechanism design.' ACM EC. https://doi.org/10.1145/3490486.3538250
key_references: Saleh (2021) RFS; Roughgarden (2021) ACM EC
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM social dilemma context.

name: Nudge & default-setting
human_example:
UK auto-enrolment pensions (2012): instead of asking people to opt into savings, they're enrolled automatically and must actively opt out. Participation jumped from ~60% to 90%+ overnight — without any new incentive.
Thaler, R. & Sunstein, C. (2008) Nudge. Penguin. Also UK Dept for Work & Pensions (2023) Auto-enrolment statistics. https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/automatic-enrolment-statistics-2023
key_references: Thaler & Sunstein (2008) Nudge; UK auto-enrolment pensions
llm_evidence: Discussed as design recommendation (Kolt 2024) but not empirically tested in LLM simulation.

name: Carrot/stick choice (Andreoni)
human_example:
A manager choosing between praising high performers vs. docking pay for low ones. Both work. Context matters: punishment edges reward in most lab settings, but reward is more effective when cooperation is already high.

Andreoni, J. et al. (2003) 'Carrot or stick.' AER. https://doi.org/10.1257/000282803321455278
llm_evidence:
✓ Directly tested — Jin lab (SanctSim). Both options available in the SI. Humans prefer punishment (ratio 1.66); all tested LLMs prefer rewards (ratio 0.00–0.88). Reasoning models (o1-series) prefer neither — they free-ride instead.
Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim — COLM 2025. https://zhijing-jin.com/files/papers/2025_SanctSim.pdf

name: Ostrom graduated sanctions (warning → fine → suspension)
human_example:
The 'yellow card' — a formal notice before any real penalty. Ostrom's research on Swiss alpine meadows and Spanish irrigation systems showed that jumping straight to fines makes people resentful and abandon the commons.

Ostrom, E. (1990) Governing the Commons. Cambridge UP. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511807763 | Fines that get heavier each time you re-offend. A Japanese fishing village studied by Ostrom charges more per kg of quota excess the second time. Makes the punishment feel earned rather than arbitrary.

Ostrom, E. (1990) ibid. Also Kuperan, K. & Sutinen, J. (1998) 'Blue water crime.' Law & Society Review. https://doi.org/10.2307/827738
key_references: Ostrom (1990) Governing the Commons; Swiss alpine meadows, Spanish irrigation
llm_evidence: SanctSim uses escalating institutional pressure; specific graduated sequence not isolated.
notes: merged Overview "Warning (1st violation)"; merged Overview "Escalating fine"

name: Graduated throttling / QoS degradation
human_example:
Mobile data slowing from full speed to 2G after you've used your monthly allowance — still usable, but degraded. Graduated response proportional to how far over the limit you've gone. No hard cutoff.

Braden, R. et al. (1994) 'Integrated services in the internet architecture: An overview.' RFC 1633. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1633
key_references: RFC 1633 (integrated services); mobile data throttling
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. GovSim's extraction ceiling is binary, not graduated.

name: Exponential back-off
human_example:
After a failed login, wait 1 second. After another failure, 2 seconds. Then 4, 8, 16... An automated escalating delay that makes brute-force attacks cost-prohibitive without blocking legitimate users permanently.

Karn, P. & Partridge, C. (1987) 'Improving round-trip time estimates in reliable transport protocols.' ACM SIGCOMM. https://doi.org/10.1145/55483.55484
key_references: Karn & Partridge (1987) SIGCOMM; TCP congestion control
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Governance graph (state machine: Warning→Suspended→Fined→Active)
human_example:
A compliance state machine: new employee → trained → certified → flagged → suspended → reinstated. Each state has defined rules and transitions enforced at runtime. Applied to AI agents by Pierucci et al. (2026).

Pierucci, F. et al. (2026) 'Governance graphs for AI agent sanctioning' (preprint). Also Ostrom, E. (1990) design principles applied to automated systems.
key_references: Pierucci et al. (2026) governance graphs (preprint)
llm_evidence: ✓ Tested. Pierucci et al. (2026): runtime governance graph outperforms prompt-only sanctioning.

name: Cheap talk / public pledge (non-binding)
human_example:
Non-binding pre-game pledges, UN declarations, or simply saying 'let's all be fair' before starting. Surprisingly effective: even cheap promises shift behaviour by creating shared expectations everyone can point to.

Sally, D. (1995) 'Conversation and cooperation in social dilemmas.' Rationality & Society. https://doi.org/10.1177/1043463195007001004
key_references: Sally (1995) Rationality & Society; Cialdini (1984) Influence; Piatti, Jin et al. (2024) GovSim
llm_evidence: ✓ Directly tested (GovSim). Communication critical for cooperation; dramatically higher survival.

name: Binding commitment device (costly to reverse)
human_example:
A savings club where you hand your money to a treasurer who won't return it until year-end. Or a pre-committed gym contract. Removes temptation by making it costly to back out — Odysseus tied to the mast.

Ashraf, N. et al. (2006) 'Tying Odysseus to the mast.' Quarterly J. of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/qjec.2006.121.2.635
key_references: Ashraf et al. (2006) QJE (Tying Odysseus to the mast)
llm_evidence: Partially tested. GovSim agents state intentions — soft commitment. Hard binding not implemented.

name: Deposit / reputation bond
human_example:
A tenant's security deposit — paid upfront, returned if you behave. Construction performance bonds work similarly. The money at stake makes your commitment credible before you've done anything.

Klein, B. & Leffler, K. (1981) 'The role of market forces in assuring contractual performance.' J. of Political Economy. https://doi.org/10.1086/261001
key_references: Klein & Leffler (1981) JPE; tenant security deposits, construction bonds
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. Escrowed upfront deposits not implemented.

name: Smart contract auto-execution
human_example:
A smart contract that releases payment to a builder automatically when a sensor confirms the building is complete — no lawyers, no court, no negotiation. The code runs itself the moment conditions are met.

Szabo, N. (1997) 'Formalizing and securing relationships on public networks.' First Monday. https://doi.org/10.5210/fm.v2i9.548
key_references: Szabo (1997) First Monday; Ethereum smart contracts
llm_evidence: Discussed (Pierucci et al. 2026) but not as blockchain smart contract per se.

name: Resource taboo / sacred no-take zone
human_example:
Traditional 'no-take' zones enforced by cultural taboo — certain days, certain waters, certain forests. Scientists have found these informal rules often outperform formal regulations in protecting shared resources.

Cinner, J. & Aswani, S. (2007) 'Integrating customary management into MPAs.' Biological Conservation. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2006.10.034
key_references: Cinner & Aswani (2007) Biological Conservation; traditional MPAs
llm_evidence: Partially tested via GovSim's hard extraction ceiling (not culturally framed).

name: Voluntary public commitment
human_example:
Making a public pledge is much harder to break than a private one. Paris Agreement signatories, fundraising challenges, and pre-commitment apps all use this. Cialdini's 'commitment & consistency' principle.

Cialdini, R. (1984) Influence. HarperCollins. Empirical: Lokhorst et al. (2013) 'Commitment and behavior change.' Environment & Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1177/0013916511411477
llm_evidence:
Partially tested. GovSim uses pre-round communication where agents state intended extraction levels — a form of public commitment. Communication was found critical for cooperation.
Piatti, Jin et al. (2024) GovSim — NeurIPS 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16698

name: Hard rate limit (API/bandwidth)
human_example:
When an app sends too many requests per second, the server simply stops responding — a hard ceiling. Prevents one user from hogging a shared resource and starving everyone else. Standard in cloud computing (AWS, Google Cloud).

Nagle, J. (1984) 'Congestion control in IP/TCP internetworks.' RFC 896. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc896
llm_evidence:
Partially tested via GovSim's extraction ceiling. Agents cannot extract beyond the group's sustainable limit; attempts cause group collapse. A hard ceiling is implicit rather than modelled as a rate-limiting mechanism per se.
Piatti, Jin et al. (2024) GovSim — NeurIPS 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16698

name: Collective punishment (all penalised for one defection)
human_example:
If one player cheats, everyone shares part of the penalty — creating strong internal pressure to self-police. Airline crew are collectively penalised if security is breached, so they monitor each other.

Olson, M. (1965) The Logic of Collective Action. Harvard UP. Also Abbink, K. et al. (2017) 'Peer punishment promotes enforcement of bad social norms.' Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms12578
key_references: Olson (1965) Logic of Collective Action; Abbink et al. (2017) Nature Comms
llm_evidence: Partially tested. SanctSim's SI creates shared-cost enforcement among members.

name: Cross-default / solidarity lending
human_example:
A credit union where one member's default raises borrowing costs for everyone — creating strong social pressure to stay current. HOA fees and solidarity lending groups (Grameen Bank) use the same mechanism.

Besley, T. & Coate, S. (1995) 'Group lending, repayment incentives, and social collateral.' J. of Development Economics. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3878(95)00005-5
key_references: Besley & Coate (1995) J Dev Econ; Grameen Bank; HOA fees
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Mutual aid pooling / decentralized bail fund
human_example:
A community bail fund pools small donations to post bail for any arrested member — no credit check, no bureaucracy. Grameen Bank solidarity groups work similarly: the group covers anyone who can't repay, creating mutual accountability.

Yunus, M. (1999) Banker to the Poor. PublicAffairs. Also Feigenberg, B. et al. (2013) 'The economic returns to social interaction.' Review of Economic Studies. https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdt016
key_references: Yunus (1999) Banker to the Poor; Feigenberg et al. (2013) REStud
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Tit-for-Tat / Win-Stay Lose-Shift
human_example:
I'll cooperate as long as you do.' Tit-for-Tat won Axelrod's famous computer tournament against hundreds of strategies. Win-Stay Lose-Shift refines it to avoid endless retaliation. The simplest conditional strategy outperforms complex ones.
Axelrod, R. (1984) The Evolution of Cooperation. Basic Books. https://www.basicbooks.com/titles/robert-axelrod/the-evolution-of-cooperation/9780465005642/
key_references: Axelrod (1984) Evolution of Cooperation; Akata et al. (2025); FAIRGAME (2025)
llm_evidence: ✓ Tested. Akata et al. (2025, Nature Human Behaviour): GPT-4 acts like harsh TFT. FAIRGAME classifies LLM strategies.

name: Threshold-based reward/punish switch
human_example:
A fishing cooperative that gives bonuses when stocks are healthy (cooperation is high) but switches to fines when stocks dip below a threshold (cooperation is low). Adapts the sanction tool to current conditions automatically.
Andreoni, J. et al. (2003) 'Carrot or stick.' AER. https://doi.org/10.1257/000282803321455278 Also Zhang, B. et al. (2025) 'Adaptive sanctioning in CPR games.' Research Policy.
key_references: Andreoni et al. (2003) AER; Zhang et al. (2025) Research Policy
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in Jin lab.

name: Pigouvian tax (externality pricing)
human_example:
A carbon tax charges companies per tonne of CO₂ emitted, making pollution expensive and nudging toward cleaner choices. Named after economist Arthur Pigou (1920). Sweden's carbon tax (over $130/tonne) is the world's highest.

Pigou, A.C. (1920) The Economics of Welfare. Macmillan. Also Nordhaus, W. (2007) 'To tax or not to tax.' Review of Environmental Economics. https://doi.org/10.1093/reep/rem008
key_references: Pigou (1920) Economics of Welfare; Nordhaus (2007); Sweden carbon tax
llm_evidence: Partially tested via GovSim's implicit extraction cost; explicit per-unit tax not implemented.

name: Reputational indirect reciprocity
human_example:
You help a stranger not because they helped you, but because others can see you helping and will trust you more later. Nowak & Sigmund call this 'image scoring' — cooperation maintained by reputation, not direct exchange.

Nowak, M. & Sigmund, K. (2005) 'Evolution of indirect reciprocity.' Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature04131
llm_evidence:
Partially tested. Image scoring is implicit in GovSim and SanctSim: agents' past records are visible and affect others' decisions. Full reputation-based exclusion without direct punishment has not been isolated.
Piatti, Jin et al. (2024) GovSim. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16698
Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim. https://zhijing-jin.com/files/papers/2025_SanctSim.pdf

name: Elected monitor / legitimate authority
human_example:
A democratically elected compliance officer gets far better cooperation than one appointed top-down. A field experiment in Uganda found elected monitors improved contribution rates significantly vs. randomly assigned ones.

Baldassarri, D. & Grossman, G. (2011) 'Centralized sanctioning and legitimate authority.' PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1105456108
key_references: Baldassarri & Grossman (2011) PNAS; Uganda field experiment
llm_evidence: Partially tested. SanctSim: all SI members can sanction; elected vs. random monitor not tested.

name: Participatory budgeting
human_example:
Porto Alegre (Brazil) from 1989 let citizens vote on how to spend part of the city budget — residents prioritised their actual neighbourhood needs. Now used in hundreds of cities worldwide. Contribution to deliberation = influence.

Wampler, B. (2007) Participatory Budgeting in Brazil. Penn State UP. https://doi.org/10.1353/wp.0.0019 Also Avritzer, L. (2009) Participatory Institutions in Democratic Brazil. Johns Hopkins UP.
key_references: Wampler (2007) Penn State UP; Porto Alegre (Brazil) 1989+
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. Agent voting on allocation rules not implemented.

name: DAO token voting & veto
human_example:
MakerDAO token holders vote on interest rates and risk parameters for its stablecoin. Token holders with bigger stakes have more votes. Democratic in theory, but large holders can dominate — a known flaw.

Buterin, V. (2014) Ethereum Whitepaper (above). Also Mehar, M. et al. (2019) 'Understanding a revolutionary enabling technology.' JCIS. https://doi.org/10.4018/JCIS.2019010101
key_references: MakerDAO governance; Buterin (2014); Mehar et al. (2019)
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM social dilemma context.

name: Institutional self-selection (choose your regime)
human_example:
People voluntarily choosing to live under stricter rules because they trust the institution. A Science paper by Gürerk et al. (2006) showed lab participants migrated toward sanctioning institutions — even from a free-rider paradise.

Gürerk, Ö. et al. (2006) 'The competitive advantage of sanctioning institutions.' Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1123633
key_references: Gürerk et al. (2006) Science; Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim
llm_evidence: ✓ Directly tested (SanctSim). Traditional LLMs adopt sanctioning institution 92.9%+; reasoning LLMs (o1-mini) only 28%.

name: Whistleblower leniency / cartel immunity
human_example:
The first cartel member to confess to antitrust authorities gets immunity from prosecution. Creates a 'race to confess' that breaks up cartels faster than any external investigation could. EU leniency programme has broken up hundreds of cartels.

European Commission Leniency Programme. https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/cartels/leniency_en
key_references: EU Leniency Programme; race to confess in antitrust
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Apology & confession as norm repair
human_example:
Corporate public apologies after scandals; Japanese corporate bowing ceremonies; Catholic confession as norm-repair ritual. Research shows a sincere apology reduces retaliatory impulse in victims even when no material compensation follows.

Tavuchis, N. (1991) Mea Culpa: A Sociology of Apology and Reconciliation. Stanford UP. Also Lazare, A. (2004) On Apology. Oxford UP. https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195156799.001.0001
key_references: Tavuchis (1991) Mea Culpa; Lazare (2004) On Apology
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. MoralSim (Backmann, Jin et al. 2025) tests moral framing but not apology mechanics.

name: Truth & reconciliation (amnesty for disclosure)
human_example:
South Africa's Truth & Reconciliation Commission offered amnesty in exchange for full public disclosure of crimes committed under apartheid. The act of honest truth-telling was itself part of the repair — not just a condition for leniency.

Tutu, D. (1999) No Future Without Forgiveness. Doubleday. Also Hayner, P. (2011) Unspeakable Truths. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203832592
key_references: South Africa TRC; Tutu (1999); Hayner (2011) Unspeakable Truths
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Material repair & restitution (restore actual harm)
human_example:
A vandal required to repaint the wall they damaged — physical restoration of actual harm, not just a fine paid into a central fund. Restorative justice research shows repair assignments reduce re-offending more than equivalent fines.

Braithwaite, J. (1989) Crime, Shame and Reintegration. Cambridge UP. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804618 | Financial compensation paid directly to the victim, not into a general fund. Court-ordered restitution in fraud cases; criminal injuries compensation boards. Keeps the focus on the person actually harmed, not the abstract rule violated.

Zehr, H. (2015) The Little Book of Restorative Justice. Good Books. Also US Crime Victims Rights Act (2004). https://www.justice.gov/usao/resources/crime-victims-rights-ombudsman/victims-rights-act
key_references: Braithwaite (1989) Crime, Shame and Reintegration; Zehr (2015) Little Book of Restorative Justice
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. Restorative mechanisms are an important open gap in LLM governance.

name: Reintegrative shaming (separate act from person)
key_references: Braithwaite (1989); Sherman & Strang (2007) Restorative Justice: The Evidence
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Rehabilitation programme (structured re-entry)
human_example:
The path back in after being suspended — conditional re-entry, parole with requirements, community reintegration programmes. Ostrom's design principles explicitly include this: the goal is restoration, not permanent exile.

Ostrom, E. (1990) ibid. Also Travis, J. (2005) But They All Come Back: Facing the Challenges of Prisoner Reentry. Urban Institute Press. | Braithwaite's 'reintegrative shaming': the offender is shamed for the act but explicitly welcomed back into the community afterward. Distinguishes the person from the behaviour — critical for keeping group membership viable and preventing permanent social exclusion.

Braithwaite, J. (1989) Crime, Shame and Reintegration. Cambridge UP. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804618 Also Sherman, L. & Strang, H. (2007) Restorative Justice: The Evidence. Smith Institute. https://www.smith-institute.org.uk/book/restorative-justice-the-evidence/ | Drug treatment courts that divert offenders into rehabilitation instead of prison; youth justice programmes addressing root causes of offending. Focus is on changing future behaviour, not punishing past behaviour. Re-offending rates significantly lower than custodial sentences.
Marlowe, D. et al. (2012) 'Adaptive interventions in drug court.' J. of Drug Issues. https://doi.org/10.1177/002204261204200305 Also SAMHSA (2023) Drug Court Best Practices. https://www.samhsa.gov/criminal-juvenile-justice/drug-courts
key_references: Ostrom (1990) design principles; drug courts; Travis (2005) But They All Come Back
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. Significant open direction for SanctSim follow-up.
notes: merged Overview "Rehabilitation & re-entry"; merged Overview "Reintegration"; merged Overview "Rehabilitation after breach"

name: Community reconciliation
human_example:
Rwanda's gacaca courts and Northern Ireland's community dialogue processes both focused on rebuilding the relationship between offender and community — not just punishing the offender. Victims reported higher satisfaction than with conventional courts.

Clark, P. (2010) The Gacaca Courts, Post-Genocide Justice and Reconciliation in Rwanda. Cambridge UP. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511761584
key_references: Rwanda gacaca courts; Clark (2010) Cambridge UP
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Metanorm: punish non-punishers
human_example:
The social expectation to call out someone who lets rule-breaking slide ('you saw what he did and said nothing?'). Axelrod showed this 'metanorm' can stabilise enforcement systems that would otherwise unravel.

Axelrod, R. (1986) 'An evolutionary approach to norms.' American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.2307/1960858
key_references: Axelrod (1986) APSR
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. Second-order enforcement not isolated in GovSim or SanctSim.

name: Anti-social punishment filter
human_example:
"In some cultures, people punish those who cooperate too much — 'tall poppy syndrome,' spite, or resentment. Herrmann et al. (2008) found this antisocial punishment in lab experiments across 16 countries. A filter prevents it from corrupting the system.

Herrmann, B. et al. (2008) 'Antisocial punishment across societies.' Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1153808"
key_references: Herrmann et al. (2008) Science (anti-social punishment across 16 countries)
llm_evidence: Not yet directly tested. SanctSim records LLMs rarely punish but no formal filter implemented.

name: Constitutional vs. operational rules (nested tiers)
human_example:
"A country's constitution vs. its everyday laws. Constitutional rules are harder to change and govern how other rules are made. Ostrom's design principle 8: stable commons governance needs these nested tiers — who decides who decides.

Ostrom, E. (1990) Governing the Commons, Ch. 6. Cambridge UP. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511807763 Also Kelsen, H. (1945) General Theory of Law and State. Harvard UP."
key_references: Ostrom (1990) Ch. 6; Kelsen (1945) General Theory of Law and State
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. Pierucci et al. (2026) governance graphs address rule hierarchies at implementation level.

name: Formal appeals & contestability
human_example:
The right to appeal a parking fine, a sacking, or an algorithmic decision — a formal check against arbitrary sanctions. GDPR Article 22 gives EU citizens the right to contest automated decisions that affect them.

GDPR Art. 22 — Automated individual decision-making. https://gdpr-info.eu/art-22-gdpr/ Also Mashaw, J. (1983) Bureaucratic Justice. Yale UP.
key_references: GDPR Art. 22; Mashaw (1983) Bureaucratic Justice
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. GDPR-style contestability noted as design challenge (Kolt 2024).

name: Mediation & arbitration
human_example:
Resolving disputes through an independent third party rather than courts — faster, cheaper, and private. The ICC handles thousands of international commercial arbitrations per year. Ostrom's design principle 6 emphasises accessible conflict resolution.

ICC International Court of Arbitration annual report 2023. https://iccwbo.org/dispute-resolution/dispute-resolution-services/arbitration/
key_references: ICC International Court of Arbitration; Ostrom design principle 6
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: False-positive correction
human_example:
A system for fixing mistakes — wrongful convictions overturned, fraud flags cleared, automated bans reversed. The Innocence Project has exonerated 200+ US prisoners through DNA evidence. Critical in AI systems that will misclassify.

Innocence Project exoneration data. https://innocenceproject.org/exoneration-data/ Also GDPR Art. 22 (above).
key_references: Innocence Project; GDPR Art. 22
llm_evidence: Not yet tested. LLMs sometimes punish high contributors in SanctSim — no correction mechanism.

name: Code-is-law vs. hard fork (social override)
human_example:
In 2016 a hacker legally drained $60M from a smart contract by exploiting its code. The Ethereum community voted to rewrite history and reverse the transaction — overriding 'code is law' via a community hard fork.

DuPont, Q. (2017) 'Experiments in algorithmic governance.' In Bitcoin and Beyond, Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315211909
key_references: 2016 DAO hack & Ethereum hard fork; DuPont (2017) Routledge
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Universalization prompting ('what if everyone did this?')
human_example: The 'what if everyone did that?' question — used by parents, teachers, and Kant's ethics alike. A 2024 AI governance study found prompting AI agents with this question improved sustainable resource choices significantly.
key_references: Piatti, Jin et al. (2024) GovSim; Kant's categorical imperative
llm_evidence: ✓ Directly tested (GovSim). Single most effective cooperation-promoting intervention found.

name: Fermi imitation (copy successful neighbours)
human_example:
Watching what your most successful colleagues do and copying their approach. Cultural evolution works the same way — we learn by imitating those who seem to be doing well. Strategy spreads through a population without central planning.

Boyd, R. & Richerson, P. (1985) Culture and the Evolutionary Process. U of Chicago Press. Also Fudenberg, D. & Levine, D. (1998) The Theory of Learning in Games. MIT Press.
key_references: Boyd & Richerson (1985) Culture and the Evolutionary Process
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in Jin lab.

name: Algorithm generation (Willis-style tournaments)
human_example:
High-frequency trading algorithms compete in financial markets — each algorithm is a strategy, and markets evolve by selecting which survive. Applied to cooperation games by Willis & Mourant to study how sanctioning strategies evolve.

Axelrod, R. (1987) 'The evolution of strategies in the iterated prisoner's dilemma.' In Davis (ed.) Genetic Algorithms and Simulated Annealing. Also Warnakulasuriya et al. (2024) algorithmic cooperation.
key_references: Axelrod (1987) genetic algorithms; Warnakulasuriya et al. (2024)
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: VCG mechanism (truthful dominant strategy)
human_example:
A special auction design (used by Google for ad slots) where telling the truth about your valuation is always your best move — the mechanism is designed so honesty dominates every other strategy. No policing needed.

Vickrey, W. (1961) 'Counterspeculation, auctions.' J. of Finance. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8276.1961.tb00412.x Also Clarke (1971), Groves (1973).
key_references: Vickrey (1961); Clarke (1971); Groves (1973); Google ad auctions
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM social dilemma context.

name: Token-curated registry (stake to challenge entries)
human_example:
A decentralized list of 'trusted' sources — anyone can challenge an entry by staking tokens. If your challenge is upheld, you earn; if it fails, you lose your stake. Crowd-sourced quality control with real financial incentives.

Simon de la Rouviere (2017) 'Token-curated registries 1.0.' Medium. https://medium.com/@ilovebagels/token-curated-registries-1-0-61a232f8dac7
key_references: de la Rouviere (2017) TCR 1.0
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Quadratic funding (anti-plutocratic matching)
key_references: Buterin et al. (2019) Management Science; Gitcoin
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Moral hazard premium
human_example:
Drivers with a history of speeding pay higher car insurance — the premium internalises the extra risk they impose on everyone else. Deductibles work similarly: you bear part of any loss, making you more careful.

Arrow, K. (1963) 'Uncertainty and the welfare economics of medical care.' AER. Also Cohen, A. & Siegelman, P. (2010) 'Testing for adverse selection.' J. of Risk & Insurance. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1539-6975.2010.01361.x
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM multi-agent systems. Variable insurance premiums based on violation history have not been implemented in published LLM cooperation research.

name: Timebanking & community currency
human_example:
A local timebank where 1 hour of babysitting earns 1 time credit — redeemable for 1 hour of someone fixing your bike. Every hour of any task is equal. Used widely in COVID-19 mutual aid networks across the UK and US.

Cahn, E. (2000) No More Throw-Away People. Essential Books. Also Collom, E. (2008) 'Motivations and participation in a community currency system.' Sociological Forum. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1573-7861.2008.00066.x | Mondragon cooperative (Spain, 80,000+ worker-owners) or LETS (Local Exchange Trading Systems) — local currencies that only circulate within the community, keeping value local and locking out free-riders from outside.

North, P. (2010) Local Money: How to Make it Happen in Your Community. Green Books. Also Gibson-Graham, J.K. (2006) A Postcapitalist Politics. U Minnesota Press.
key_references: Cahn (2000) No More Throw-Away People; LETS systems; Mondragon
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.
notes: merged Overview "Timebanking (service credits)"; merged Overview "Barter & community currency"

name: Generalised reciprocity / gift economy
human_example:
Open-source software — you contribute code, someone else benefits, someone else contributes back, with no direct exchange. Wikipedia works the same way. Kropotkin argued this gift-economy logic was the original human economy.

Kropotkin, P. (1902) Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution. McClure Phillips. Also Benkler, Y. (2006) The Wealth of Networks. Yale UP. https://cyber.harvard.edu/wealth_of_networks/
key_references: Kropotkin (1902) Mutual Aid; Benkler (2006) Wealth of Networks; open-source software
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Network embeddedness / social capital (Putnam)
human_example:
Why do regions with lots of civic clubs (choirs, sports leagues, neighbourhood associations) end up with better-functioning governments and less corruption? Putnam's landmark Italian study: dense social networks build generalised trust.

Putnam, R. (1993) Making Democracy Work: Civic Traditions in Modern Italy. Princeton UP. https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691037387/making-democracy-work
key_references: Putnam (1993) Making Democracy Work; Baldassarri (2015) AJS
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Worker cooperative (ownership as incentive alignment)
human_example:
At Mondragon every worker owns part of the cooperative and gets one vote regardless of seniority. Profits are shared. Incentives align because everyone's success depends on collective effort — ownership replaces punishment.

Whyte, W. & Whyte, K. (1991) Making Mondragon: The Growth and Dynamics of the Worker Cooperative Complex. ILR Press. Also Pencavel, J. (2013) 'The economics of worker cooperatives.' JEEA. https://doi.org/10.1111/jeea.12023
key_references: Mondragon; Pencavel (2013) JEEA; Whyte & Whyte (1991)
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.
notes: merged Overview "Worker cooperative (one worker, one vote)"

name: Mesh network / offline resilience
human_example:
Meshtastic devices used in disaster zones (California wildfires, Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria) keep communications alive when phone towers fail — a peer-to-peer radio mesh that anyone can join and relay.

Vega, D. et al. (2012) 'A survey on decentralized wireless mesh networks.' IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials. https://doi.org/10.1109/SURV.2011.100811.00062
key_references: Meshtastic; Vega et al. (2012) IEEE; Puerto Rico post-Maria
llm_evidence: Not yet tested.

name: Solidarity & mutual accountability
human_example:
A mutual aid group where members check in on each other, call each other out gently when something is wrong, and share responsibility — no boss, no formal rules. Horizontal accountability between equals.

Spade, D. (2020) Mutual Aid: Building Solidarity During This Crisis (And the Next). Verso. Also Baldassarri, D. (2015) 'Cooperative networks.' American J. of Sociology. https://doi.org/10.1086/683945
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM multi-agent systems. Horizontal mutual accountability without formal sanctions has not been isolated as a mechanism in published LLM research.

name: Blockchain-based mutual aid DAO
human_example:
Gitcoin's quadratic funding gives proportionally more weight to many small donors than to one large donor — making it harder for wealthy actors to dominate community funding decisions. Anti-plutocratic by design.

Buterin, V. et al. (2019) 'A flexible design for funding public goods.' Management Science. https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2019.3337
llm_evidence: Not yet tested in LLM multi-agent systems. Quadratic funding mechanisms for LLM agent cooperation have not been implemented in published experiments.
